head: Code
Meaning
rows: Adds the new timestamp to the right (newest end)
Counts the requests still inside the window

p: Requests arrive at `ping(1)`, `ping(100)`, `ping(3001)`, `ping(3002)`. After each ping the valid range is `[t-3000, t]`; anything older than the range is removed from the left.
More than one timestamp can expire at once. Take `q = [1, 100, 200, 300, 5000]` and `t = 5000`; the valid range is `[2000, 5000]`, so all four older timestamps must go.
With `if` you would remove only `1` and still return a wrong count. With `while` you keep removing from the left until the oldest remaining timestamp is valid.

blocks.h: Why a deque instead of a list?
p: We add new timestamps at one end and remove old ones from the other, which is exactly what a deque is built for.

bullets: Time: O(1) amortized per `ping()`. Each timestamp is appended once and removed at most once. A single call can take O(n) if it removes many old timestamps.
Space: O(n), where n is the most timestamps held in the queue at once.

p: The code reads `self.q[0]` without checking the queue is nonempty. That is safe here because `ping()` always appends the current timestamp first, and timestamps arrive in strictly increasing order, so the loop can never empty the queue.

933.takeaway: This is a sliding time window implemented with a queue. When events arrive in time order and you must drop old events while keeping recent ones, a deque is usually the right tool.
